say.en: Your phone shows a cricket score from a match in Melbourne within a second. Millions of computers passed that score along. How did this world-wide web of machines begin? In this lesson: Define a computer network and node.
List benefits of networking.
Trace key milestones from ARPANET to the web.

body.en: A *computer network* is an interconnection of two or more computing devices (nodes or hosts) that share data and resources. Nodes communicate through wired or wireless media, sending data in small units called packets. Networks let us share printers, files and Internet connections, and communicate by e-mail, chat and video calls.

narration.en: A computer network connects two or more devices so they can share data and resources. Data travels in small pieces called packets.

title.en: On the board: From ARPANET to the Internet

say.en: A network joins two or more devices so that they can share data and resources, such as a printer.
Data travels in small units called packets.
It began in 1969 with ARPANET linking a few computers in the USA. E-mail came in 1971.
TCP/IP was proposed in 1974 and became the standard in 1983. Tim Berners-Lee created the World Wide Web around 1990.
Today Wi-Fi, mobile data and the Internet of Things connect billions of devices.

prompt.en: Put these milestones of networking in time order.

steps.en: 1969: ARPANET links a few university and research computers in the USA
1971: Ray Tomlinson sends the first network e-mail
1983: TCP/IP becomes the standard of ARPANET
Mid-1980s: NSFNET links universities and DNS is introduced
1989–90: Tim Berners-Lee develops the World Wide Web at CERN

explanation.en: ARPANET came first, then e-mail, then the TCP/IP protocols that became its standard, then NSFNET and DNS, and finally the Web, which runs on top of the Internet.

say.en: How networking grew Put these milestones of networking in time order.

body.en: 1969: ARPANET connects a few university and research computers in the USA. 1971: Ray Tomlinson sends the first network e-mail. 1974: TCP/IP is proposed, and it became ARPANET's standard in 1983. Mid-1980s: NSFNET links universities; the Domain Name System is introduced. 1989–90: Tim Berners-Lee develops the World Wide Web at CERN. Since then, Wi-Fi, mobile data and the Internet of Things have connected billions of devices.

heading.en: Evolution, Data Communication and Transmission Media

tagline.en: ARPANET to the Internet, the five components of data communication, bandwidth and data transfer rate, IP and MAC addresses, circuit and packet switching, and wired and wireless media.

myth.en: Bandwidth and data transfer rate are the same thing, both measured in Mbps.

truth.en: Bandwidth is the range of frequencies the channel can carry (Hz). Data transfer rate is the number of bits actually sent per second (bps). Higher bandwidth allows a higher data rate, but they are different quantities. Internet plans are sold as "bandwidth: 100 Mbps", so everyday speech mixes them. The board expects the textbook distinction and the right units.

say.en: ARPANET (1969) → NSFNET (1986) → the Internet, a network of networks.
Five components: sender, receiver, message, medium, protocol.
Bandwidth in Hz; data transfer rate in bps; 1 byte = 8 bits.
Circuit switching reserves a path; packet switching routes packets independently.
Wired: twisted pair, coaxial, optical fibre. Wireless: radio, microwave, infrared.

goal.en: ARPANET to the Internet, the five components of data communication, bandwidth and data transfer rate, IP and MAC addresses, circuit and packet switching, and wired and wireless media.

question.en: Which switching technique does the Internet use?

explain.en: Data is split into packets that are routed independently.

task.en: Match each need to the best medium.

explain.en: Fibre for huge bandwidth over distance, twisted pair for low cost, infrared for short line-of-sight, microwave for tower links, radio for signals that must pass through walls.

takeaway.en: ARPANET (1969) → NSFNET (1986) → the Internet, a network of networks.

narration.en: Many people think: Bandwidth and data transfer rate are the same thing, both measured in Mbps. Actually: Bandwidth is the range of frequencies the channel can carry (Hz). Data transfer rate is the number of bits actually sent per second (bps). Higher bandwidth allows a higher data rate, but they are different quantities. Internet plans are sold as "bandwidth: 100 Mbps", so everyday speech mixes them. The board expects the textbook distinction and the right units.

problem.en: List the network resources shared in your college computer lab and say what would happen without a network.

steps.en: Internet connection: one broadband line is shared by everyone.
Files: the lecturer shares practical files from one server.
Without a network, each computer would need its own printer and connection, and files would move by pen drive.

answer.en: Printer, Internet and files are shared; without a network, cost and effort rise sharply.
